Protecting Yourself from Hypnotists

Hypnotism can happen in a therapist’s office, but it can also happen through music, marketing, religious rituals, sexual chemistry, charismatic authority, social media, grief, fear, political messaging, sense of belonging, fatigue, love, trauma, beauty, etc.

Even when not actively engaging the conscious mind, there are many ways to influence people. Marketers and interface designers know this perfectly well. In the Federal Trade Commission’s report on “dark patterns,” they describe designs that trick or manipulate consumers. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) describes commercial patterns that steer, deceive, coerce, or manipulate people toward choices that may work against their interests.

Conscious agreement, unconscious receptivity, emotional compliance, legal and ethical consent: those are all different things. Someone’s mind can be influenced without their adult self having clearly chosen the influence.

As a line associated with the Silva Mind Control tradition puts it,

“If you don’t learn to control your mind, someone else will!”

Since there are a lot of forces out there already training your mind, via ads, fear, craving, screens, tribe, resentment, authority, loneliness, and repetition, you can use self-hypnosis techniques to work from the inside: befriend your deeper mind, listen closely, and make it easier to choose things for yourself as an adult.

Hypnosis Evidence

Is there REAL (not magical) evidence for Hypnosis? Yes. In 2024 there has been an overview of 49 meta analyses containing a total of 261 distinct primary studies. Evidence was strongest for pain, medical procedures, and work with children and adolescents, but varied with different outcomes and study design quality.

Is there evidence for Self-Hypnosis? Yes. There has been a systematic review of Randomized Controlled Trials of self-hypnosis, finding benefit in studies of pain, child birth, pediatric, stress, anxiety etc. Self-hypnosis seemed more useful when done as a real self-skill several times, not just listening to an audio file.

Here I will be teaching you a real self-skill, so you don’t end up a consumer of more and more elaborate trance recordings.

Mayo Clinic cautions that using hypnosis around stressful earlier-life events can trigger strong emotional reactions, and that other treatments may be better for historical trauma.

Use Self-Hypnosis for: regulation, dialogue, reparenting, clarity, habit change, present life safety, emotional integration, ordinary-life action

Don't use Self-Hypnosis for: forcing trauma memories, proof of trauma memories, suppressing medical symptoms, destabilizing yourself, instead of correct treatment

Forget the left-brain/right-brain cartoon

“Syncing the hemispheres” can be a very useful description of how the state feels, but I don’t want to over-interpret what is going on neuroscientifically. A large resting state fMRI study of 1011 people did not support the common pop- neuropsychological notion that people in general can be left or right brained, although there is certainly evidence for the lateralization of some functions or networks.

The invitation is to elicit a high level of cooperation between the verbal, analytical, imaginal, emotional, somatic, intuitive, relational, and spiritual modes. It’s not an electoral process; nobody needs to win!

The mind of love retains its warmth, the mind of analysis its brightness. The mind of intuition offers its signals without becoming dogma. The mind of rationality tests the signals without killing them. The body has a voice- it can say yes, no or not yet. The imagination has opened the field and the adult chooses the next real action. There is peace but there is also precision.

Love without analysis can become fantasy, analysis without love can become sterile. Intuition without testing can become delusion; testing without intuition can become dead. These modes can each serve to correct the others.

And of course it’s got to lead somewhere! A powerful state only matters if something survives it: kinder behavior, more humility, better judgment, real service, or a more workable ordinary life.

When “your voice” is everybody else’s voice

Working with your inner child can be harder when your private self had very little room to develop. This can happen when people come from a background where their family, religion or community took over their life very early on, or they were pressured to achieve in a certain way at a young age. This means that you don’t know what you feel, what you want, what you believe, what you like, or what you don’t like until you hear what someone else says first. This makes it hard to follow the advice to “love yourself” when you don’t know who “yourself” is. So in these cases, reparenting can go hand in hand with finding yourself. For some, it’s easy to work with their child-self because they can feel their child-self really easily. For others, creating enough safety for preference, curiosity, and experimentation is part of how their child-self becomes easier to hear.

You might be in this camp if:

You don’t know what you want until you hear what someone else wants

You find that your opinions change dramatically depending on who is around

You agree with someone in the moment and later realize you didn’t agree

You tend to take responsibility for other people’s emotions to the point of erasing yourself

Trying to love yourself feels like a performance

Trying to find out how your inner child feels, results in guesses instead of feeling

You find that you can rebel, but you can’t choose

A useful way to explain this is that you may have had less room to explore “what do I like?”, “what do I want to try out?” or “who am I when nobody is grading me?”, because as a child your attention went into avoiding pain, reading danger, meeting expectations and keeping the bond. (That’s a practical model, not a claim about one specific brain system.)

Sometimes it helps to distance yourself for a certain period from the people or group that you are getting your answers from, so quieter preferences can surface. However, don’t do this for long (staying isolated would defeat the purpose) – just long enough to differentiate what is yours from what is social.

The difference between a “human doer” and a “human being” helps here. If you don’t feel like you are good enough just because you exist, you will try to create a sense of worth by being beautiful, by doing something well, by being smart, by gaining status, by being spiritual, or by being needed. These can all be real gifts. They turn into a bargain with yourself when failing at them feels like losing yourself – that as long as you are good at something (or good at being good for other people), you will be good enough to belong.

To help you find yourself, ask yourself these questions:

What do I like when no one is watching?

What do I believe before I check what other people think?

What do I want that is not in rebellion to others, and is not in compliance with others?

Where am I buying my sense of belonging by betraying myself?

What “arena” am I using to try to buy my sense of belonging?

What can I try on for size that I don’t need to impress anyone with?

What relationships allow me to be myself?

What do I notice in my body and what meaning am I attaching to it?

Give your inner child a small experiment with no value towards your resume – painting, dancing, gardening, learning a language, a sport, volunteering, playing music, or anything else you’re allowed to be bad at. The parent voice you inherited may be telling you that you are supposed to be good at something as soon as you start doing it. The adult can answer, “We’re finding out whether we enjoy this, not proving our worth.” And give it enough tries to get past the humiliation of being a beginner.

For a child, belonging can feel like survival. So families, religions, romantic relationships, political tribes, spiritual groups, institutions, and even online communities can reach astonishingly far into who you are. Part of “adulting” is finding out where you are trading your sense of self in exchange for belonging, and then consciously choosing where you want to belong – on your terms, and learning that you can disappoint someone without disappearing. A large part of your subconscious mind is made up of the voices of other people, which is why this belongs in a self-hypnosis guide.

Where am I betraying myself in exchange for belonging?

What would it feel like to belong without having to betray myself?

Is this my own guidance or a belonging program I adopted?

Is this love, or is it a fear of being excluded?

Is this my conscience or is it conditioning?

Is this devotion, or is it compliance?

Is this rebellion, or is it freedom?

Then see what your body tells you. It isn’t always right, but it deserves a seat at the hearing.

Come all the way back

Come out of the session by reversing the entry method; if you floated, come back down by the same method; land with your chosen weight. If you shrunk, come back to your normal size. If you meet your younger self or parts, make sure that you acknowledge that you are now whole, this is your body, and you are using your adult judgement. If you traveled, then come back the same way you left. Make sure that you are only bringing back what you had intended to bring back.

Say, “I am bringing back only what is useful now. All that is not needed at this time will remain safely stored away until such time as I am ready. I am now coming back to this place and to my body and to normal day to day living, and to one honest action. All instructions to go deeper or stay in this session are now over. I keep only the ordinary-life intention or future-practice cue I consciously chose, and neither one keeps today’s altered state running. I am myself, in my body, with my adult judgment fully available.”

Count yourself out: 1. Coming back into your body and your chosen weight. 2. Coming back to your normal breathing pattern. 3. Hearing the room, and naming where you are. 4. Moving your fingers and your toes and your shoulders and your eyes. 5. Opening your eyes, feeling present, normal and clear. Your session is now over.

Say to yourself what day it is or what the date is, look to your left and to your right, look at something near and something far away, move about a bit before you stand up, stand up only when you’re steady, and make sure that you are actually oriented and alert (repeating the count isn’t proof that you’re all the way back). Take note of only what actually came up during your session and what you may or may not need to do as a result, and then just go about doing something normal.

In the event that a recording that you are listening to stops unexpectedly, simply say to yourself “the recording has stopped and the session is over” and then use the above method to come out by opening your eyes, saying where you are, saying what day it is, pushing down with your feet or your hands, moving about, looking around and then using the 5 step method. Don’t sit there waiting for the voice to come back and release you.

Note: If you are using a recording to go to sleep, then it is all right to let the recording put you to sleep or have you in a quiet resting state. However, if it’s a recording for waking practice, then it should not leave you in a role, with lowered judgement, impaired movement capabilities, blank, with an undefined reset word, or invited to stay altered indefinitely.

The actual inner meeting

If you tend to daydream, dissociate or fall asleep, sit up rather than lying down for this exercise. Save lying down for when you’re ready to go to sleep or receive deep rest or are trying to incubate dreams. Keep your spine straight, but not rigid, like a soldier. Relax your jaw and maintain some connection with the room you are in.

You can say to yourself, “I am not leaving life. I am listening more deeply to life.”

Invoking: “Higher Self, universal heart-mind, wise subconscious mind, the intelligence in my body, my inner child, my inner adults, my protective parts, and all that serves truth and love: please help me understand what I need to know, only in the form and timing that is useful, kind, stabilizing and real.”

You’re asking your conscious mind to listen without forcing an answer.

This doesn’t mean you have to silence your thoughts to listen. Notice your thoughts, sensations, images, doubts, emotions, etc., without fighting them, without going with them, while you hold the intention of this exercise lightly in the background of your mind. Notice what stands out on its own.

You can say, “Tell me what I need to know or ask me what you need to know, and I will sit in silence for five minutes and listen.”

You might hear a phrase, feel a sensation, notice a memory, see a color, be contacted by a child or protector, feel pain, warmth, silence or know that you need to do something or be grateful for something or feel an urge to stop, or realize that this is enough listening for today.

Listen to it all and believe none of it automatically.

The 15-minute daily practice

You don't need to learn a second script for this: it's the same practice (gather attention, listen, respond, wait, return). Fifteen minutes or so is just a convenient appointment with yourself, not a therapeutic dose or a timetable your feelings have to follow. It's enough time to induce yourself (a few minutes), let the middle unfold at its own pace (five minutes of sitting in silence and listening is there when it's useful), and then bring yourself back out again (several minutes). You can interrupt the listening at any time to change direction.

Another simple way in: notice three things you can see, then three things you can hear and three sensations you can feel in your body. Now do two of each, then one of each. Count from 5 to 1 and start listening. Pick the entry that suits you, don't stack inductions.

After practicing a few times with a recording, feel free to cut it down to the cues you still need. Then try practicing without playing it back. But keep using recordings if you enjoy them: being independent means you can guide yourself, not that you have to refuse help. (Note: the optional re-entry cue can shorten an induction you already know well.)

When you come out of the process, ask what needed warmth, what needed protection, and what direction serves truth and love and life. Perhaps there is something to explore, or capacity to build. And what can you carry yourself now? If there is something you need to do, then make a plan with yourself to do that thing. Be concrete and say something like, "If _________ (cue) happens, then I will do ________ (one small action)." Then see how things are later on: how you are sleeping, relating and functioning, not only how impressive the session felt.

Capacity before content

NOTE: If it is medically unsafe for you to do this, or you are panicking, sleep deprived, nauseated, deeply destabilized, manic, in a psychosis-like state, or overwhelmed by chemicals, please stabilize first before seeking out what your subconscious needs you to know. It is not ready for you to know directly if it requires you to destabilize to know it! Ask for capacity, not content.

There are times when your subconscious seems to know something that your conscious mind can’t handle yet. It may be about your sexuality, a grief, trauma, your family, betrayal, shame, vocation, a relationship, fears about illness, spirituality, an addiction, your identity, or a moral issue.

What you don’t want to do is bully your subconscious with statements like,

“Why don’t you just tell me?” “What are you hiding?” “Tell me right now!” or “I demand that you reveal the truth!”

This can lead to flooding, panic, false certainty, confabulation, dissociation, and just generally making your day suck more. When you’re flooded, it can be hard to access your adult capacities to pause, compare options, reality test, plan and make choices for yourself. In that state, regulation and support come before going deeper. The silence may be protecting you while your adult doesn’t have enough regulation, support, humility or practical capacity to take it in. Ask for the next piece you can tolerate:

“Do I need to know the content now, or do I need to build capacity first?” “What would make the conscious mind 5% more able to receive this?” “Can you tell me through a symbol, not the whole revelation?” “Can you tell me what you need me to do to be safe without telling me what it is?” “Do you need me to get support to be able to know what it is? Who?”

A safer script: “Dear wise subconscious mind, if there is something you know that my conscious mind can’t handle, please don’t break it open violently. Help me become someone who can know it safely. Prepare me before you reveal it, ground me before the memory, support me before the intensity. Give me one next thing to do.”

REMEMBER: Hypnotic imagery can mean something without being literal, especially around trauma and memory. The mind turns things into symbols, squashes them together, distorts and dramatizes them, and borrows from culture and fear. Treat an image as an image, and get outside support when you need it.

What not to do

DO NOT: Treat inner voices, images, autonomous movements or body signals as commands or proof. Listen, then always reality test them.

DO NOT chase grand “downloads” or make a hobby of demons, jinn, “Unattached Burdens”, etc. Stabilize yourself first. Get help if necessary, especially if not reality testing well or if not functioning well in life.

DO NOT do self-hypnosis while driving a car, bathing, swimming, operating equipment, supervising children, or otherwise doing something that requires active attention.

DO NOT try to “force” memories, use trance to “prove” what happened, or ignore medical symptoms by “forcing” them down through hypnosis.

DO NOT “force” yourself to ignore basic body signals, like hunger, tiredness, pain, etc., or basic emotions, like grief, anger, fear, etc., before you understand what the signal is saying.

DO NOT “extend” altered states indefinitely or take intuitive hits as “real” without reality testing them.

DO NOT allow any inner role, like the “Inner Child” or “Protector” or “Nurturer” or “Leader” to get out of proportion. The child doesn’t run adult life, the Protector can’t shut out all love, the Nurturer can’t erase consequences, the Leader can’t skip over the child, and both analysis and tenderness stay available.

DO NOT use NLP techniques to “force” down “protectors” or to manufacture certainty, manipulate people, or “heal” something when the body is saying no.

Don’t convince yourself that negative indicators like doubt, distraction, resistance, or lack of response, or saying “No” are good indicators that the induction is working.

Don’t rely solely upon the “safety” of “the unconscious mind”. Always make certain you have clear limits, a safe setting, the ability to stop, and a way out you’ve tested.

Don’t believe that normal physical sensations prove hidden trauma, illness, body toxins, possession, “attachments”, “transformations” or some hidden “subconscious” truth.

Don’t believe that anything is “healed” physically or neurologically/cellularly, simply because it is “healed” in the imagination.

Don’t put in, or let anyone put in, hidden “commands”. A cue you choose consciously to reuse should have a clear purpose, stay reviewable, and be removed if you no longer want it. Just saying “cancel” doesn’t guarantee it’s instantly erased. Don’t allow anyone to put in undisclosed third-party activation, or to make YOU do anything or change to a different person or have amnesia, etc.

DO bring yourself all the way back at the end of every waking session: yourself again, moving, oriented, with your judgment back, and say straight out that the session has ended.

When this needs more support than a guide can provide

Self-hypnosis is a relationship you have with yourself, and when the situation needs actual care, this guide shouldn’t stand in for it.

Get urgent help now if you’re in immediate danger, severely confused, unable to keep yourself safe, or experiencing physical symptoms like chest pain or fainting. If you’re experiencing new or worsening suicidal thoughts, severe insomnia, or symptoms of mania or psychosis, or if your dissociative symptoms are impacting your functioning, please get them assessed by a professional promptly, rather than trying to fix them with this 4- to 12-week practice.

On the other hand, you may need very little more support. Start small—do shorter practices, make them warm, choose a small and tractable subject to work with, make sure you’re coming all the way back out of hypnosis, and track the effect on one target area (anxiety, daydreaming, repairing a relationship, an avoided task, sleep, emotional regulation, intuitive accuracy, etc.) for a week or two. If you find that your functioning worsens or you’re gaining certainty about memories that can’t be verified, then it’s time to reassess, not to push harder.

Get the right kind of ongoing help if you’re dealing with recurring panic attacks, compulsive behaviors, substance-related destabilization, or major relationship instability.

Methods to explore with a trained person present

If you want to do deliberate trauma-focused regression, to follow an affect or somatic bridge to unknown traumatic origins, or to work with substantial flashbacks or dissociative reactions, work with a trauma-informed trained clinician who is trained in the method you’re using and who is present while you do it. (Affect and somatic bridges mean following associations from an emotional or bodily feeling; regression means remembering or imagining what it would have been like when you were younger. Both can have other uses too, like finding resources.) Ask what they intend to do and how they’ll handle uncertainty and unexpected reactions. Even if you work with a clinician, please note that hypnosis can’t prove what happened in your life.

Having a history of trauma, crying, or even wanting to feel difficult feelings, doesn’t necessarily mean you need more support than working on your own. It is up to you to find how wide or narrow a range to work in, and that will be different for different people. Watch how you actually respond and what support you have. Feeling confident doesn’t make up for support you don’t have.

Major trauma guidelines emphasize treatments like trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy variants, cognitive processing therapy, prolonged exposure, or eye movement desensitization and reprocessing, depending on the person and the guideline. Self-hypnosis and inner child work can be part of that process. If you’re working with high-risk trauma, you need a bigger container for that work.

The ultimate feedback on whether your process is working well is how you’re functioning in ordinary life. If you’re being more loving, honest, functional, relational, grounded, and precise than you were before you started, then keep going, gently. If ordinary life is getting less stable, then stop trying to go deeper and focus instead on getting enough sleep, eating, grounding yourself, maintaining healthy boundaries with others, and getting support from others.

Appendix E: Is the daydream helping or replacing your life?

Sometimes, daydreaming is intuitive. Your subconscious is simulating an idea or event to help you digest grief or teach you something. The act of daydreaming may also be a creative exercise or a way your subconscious is showing you a possible future. Sometimes your subconscious will show you things you’re afraid of. Sometimes it shows you what you want.

Other times, it’s a detriment. An escape from reality. An addiction to fantasy rather than reality. Dissociation. Obsession with romantic partners. An escape hatch from adult life.

How do you know which one it is? Ask yourself, “Is my daydreaming bringing me back into life with more clarity, love and action, or pulling me away from it into repetition, craving and avoidance?”

If it’s helping you, ask: “What is the guidance inside this?”

If it’s taking you away from life, change your body before you start arguing with the story: sit up straight, open your eyes a little, feel your feet. Then ask your subconscious for help. “Hey subconscious, thanks for all these interesting images. If they’re helpful, please show me the guidance inside them. If they’re just a way for me to avoid dealing with life, please bring me gently into the present and help me deal with what I need to deal with in a gentle but structured way.”

Then get embarrassingly practical and ask yourself, “What real-life action is this daydream replacing?”

It could be anything from “send a text message” or “stop sending text messages” to “clean my room” or “eat” or “sleep” or “deal with my grief” or “create something” or “apologize” or “leave” or “tell the truth” or “make a plan” or “get help” or “return to the task at hand” or “stop chasing unavailable love.”

Appendix G: Altered states

I am NOT telling anyone to use substances. However, many people do attempt their first self-hypnosis, contact with their inner child or contact with their Higher Self while in a mind altered state.

Either way, please be aware that you should not use this state to force a revelation, but rather use it to deepen your listening, strengthen your love and improve your ordinary life.

A past opening can be a resource without becoming a state you have to keep reproducing. The key is that though it is great that this opened, it is different to have had the experience of love, to be able to access it only in a particular state and to be able to access it reliably on a day to day basis. Let the experience widen what seems possible while you build access you can actually use. If the child can't take it in, meet that difficulty rather than turning up the intensity.

So during or after an altered state, rather than asking for a revelation, you may want to use these phrases: Help me to ground. Help me to only take that which I can integrate. Help me to remember love. Help me to come back again when the time is right. Help me to turn this into one change in my regular life.

You should not use self-hypnosis to keep you in an altered state forever, to recover memories, to make you more afraid, to help you not sleep, to override medical needs, or to not communicate with other people.

If you find that being in an altered state is helping you to love less, to be more ungrounded, to be less honest, to not sleep, to not communicate or to not do regular life things, then you should stop attempting to go deeper and instead work on integrating what you have.

Stabilize before you interpret

Self-hypnosis can be extremely powerful when used in altered states of consciousness such as when one is on loveyhuasca, meditating, in a lucid dream, grieving, utilizing sexual energy, praying, not sleeping, or in other states similar to plant medicines. Sometimes the mind opens up faster than the adult self can organize what’s coming in.

The problem is that people think that because they are in an altered state, that it must mean something. Sometimes it is your inner child talking, sometimes it is a Protector showing fear, and sometimes it is shame/grief/anger/longing or other buried material asking for care, but it can also just be your body being overloaded by the experience, the chaos of the environment, lack of sleep, or some other reason that it just doesn't make sense. Just because you had a picture that scared you doesn't mean it's true, just because you had a bad feeling doesn't mean it's a lesson and just because you had a download in a nice lighting doesn't mean you should believe it.

Before trying to interpret what is happening in an altered state, ask a simpler question:

“What kind of problem is happening?”

A useful map of the mind

In this guide, when I refer to your ‘subconscious’ I am referring to the deeper processes shaping perceptions, emotions, desires, avoidance, imagery, memories, body signals, habits, intuitions, automatic behaviours etc. Sometimes it is useful to work with all of these as one ‘mind’, other times it can be more effective to work with the ‘ecology’ of parts. Neither way is ‘right’ or ‘wrong’ they’re both maps, and neither one needs its own priesthood.

Working with parts is about precision, working with the Higher Self is about coherence – and communion is the movement between them.

When you need coherence, work with the ‘whole’ – the subconscious as one:

“Invoke” the subconscious – e.g. ‘Hello wise subconscious can you help me understand…..’

When you need precision, recognise the ‘ecology’ in the subconscious – there may be a child part that wants love, a protector part that wants to keep you safe, a ‘critic’ that wants you to live up to certain standards, a fantasy making part that wants possibility, body memory that wants recognition, a social part that wants belonging, a spiritual part that wants to connect to God/source/do what is in the best benefit of all beings, a ‘wiser’ part that wants what is true, etc etc

When things feel scattered, it is a good idea to start with unity:

“Invoke” your Higher Self – e.g. ‘Hello my Higher Self/universal heart-mind/wise subconscious please guide me.’

Then move into differentiation if needed:

Ask “Which part is afraid? Which part is protecting? Which part is avoiding? Which part knows what to do? Which part is too young for this?”

Then move back into unity: “Let all of this belong to one life. Let the adult self lead with love.”

Sometimes start with the whole

Some people feel more fragmented when they start by naming 12 parts and giving everybody an office. For these people, it is better to start from the Sacred whole.

You can start like this: ‘I begin from the universal heart. I begin from Higher Self. I begin from the part of me that belongs to life before it belongs to any wound, role, family, group, identity, ideology or story. Please help me understand what is true, kind, timely, stabilizing and useful.’

Sometimes you won’t have access to your Higher Self, or to the universal heart, or whatever language feels sacred for you, or it feels borrowed from somebody else. In that case, just begin by witnessing: notice the room, your body, and that you’re in a younger state. The fact that something in you can notice is enough of an adult function to begin with.

Once you can notice, and distinguish, you don’t need to keep rehearsing the Witness. Begin working on whatever is actually missing: warmth, protection, direction etc. So while the language of the Higher Self can help you gather around a meaningful source of care, it doesn’t mean that a perfectly capable inner parent is already there. The adult functions still grow through practice.

Differentiate only when something specific comes up. “Is this coming from my inner child? Is it a protector? Is this my body speaking? Is this fear speaking? Is this intuition? Is this social conditioning speaking? Is this divine guidance or my interpretation of guidance?”

But always start from the heart, differentiate as needed, and then come back to the heart.

The inner child, the guards, and the three inner adults

Your inner child won’t trust you right away. It’s not going to be enough for you to meditate, say three nice sentences to the inner child and expect to have its trust. What’s going to help your inner child to trust you is you, the person you are right now, becoming reliable.

Here I’m going to talk about what you need to develop in yourself in order to be able to reparent your inner child. I’m going to talk about it in terms of three aspects: your Nurturer, your Protector and your Leader/Guru, but I don’t mean them as if there were really three people in you. It’s you that needs to develop these qualities.

Also, your inner child’s worth is not dependent on these qualities… It has its own worth, and its own qualities, like playing, being tender, not taking life too seriously, being creative and wondering at the world. Those belong in your relationship with it too, not just the wounds.

When the adult role is not available yet

The problem is, that some people do not have access to their adult functions at will. Instead, they may go blank, access an inherited inner critic, or feel like a child part who may be playing at being an adult. Telling them to just access their adult is like telling them to just be able to fly.

For that starting point, I use a provisional bridge I developed and call borrowed adulthood. Please note, it puts together familiar practices (witnessing, modeling, supported action, and handing over responsibility bit by bit), and I’m not claiming that the entirety of the steps has been validated as one treatment.

- Access a witnessing position, if necessary: notice what’s there without demanding warmth, wisdom or certainty. If you already know how to distinguish your internal positions, skip to the next step and access the adult position you need.

- Borrow an adult function. You may “borrow” this from a safe adult in your life, a mentor, an older sibling, a future version of yourself, a spiritual figure, a value, or even a written plan. Borrow only what you need right now – warmth, a boundary or direction.

- Put on the adult hat as an apprentice. Now, in this position, figure out what you would want to say or do – and then do at least a part of that.

- Return the adult hat, noticing what you borrowed and what you were able to do on your own (even if it’s only 5%).

This is a borrowed figure, so you’re still making the choice. The longer version of this exercise can be found in my Inner Child Self-Love Reparenting Guide .

You don’t have to have trustworthy people in your history. Use someone you remember when that helps, or just imagine a good adult whose intention is to take good care of you. See if you can imagine what they would say/do in your situation, with your history, limitations, options, etc. If you can’t imagine good, start with the least cruel response you can believe. Once you’ve found something good, try it, don’t keep doing the exercise.

It can be helpful to use borrowing when you’re in the adult position and not knowing what a decent adult would do, especially when the child doesn’t trust you and every response you can think of is retaliating, defending your goodness, collapsing or leaving. How would a decent adult hear that distrust? Borrow that one response. You may still feel young when you do it, it’s okay, feeling like an adult can come after you act like one.

Let the child speak without handing over the steering wheel

You can let those younger states talk and still keep your adult judgement. You don't have to turn that judgement over to someone else or literally become younger. You just get to tap into those feelings of wonder, play, sensation, vulnerability, honest need, or the wish to carry fewer decisions, while the adult in you stays present.

"It is okay for a younger part of me to talk. But I understand that the adult in me is always going to be here, listening, evaluating, protecting me and stopping me if needed. I am not going to replace my adult judgement with any child state, guide, recording or person."

This way you get the benefits of being young; curiosity, spontaneity, play, sensation, the ability to state your needs, to feel easily etc without any of the negatives of being a child, like obeying, being helpless, being scolded, the lack of good judgement etc.

Love doesn’t have to wait for trust

If the younger part doesn’t believe you love it yet, you can still love it, when that love is there for you to give. Its trust can question your promises, remember the times you didn’t protect it, and take its time. The love can stay while that happens.

You can start with something like, “Okay. I believe that you don’t believe me. I still love you though. You don’t have to love me back. Tell me what doesn’t feel safe to you.”

That isn’t a way to end the complaint. Hear the truth in it and answer it seriously. Hearing anger without hitting back, admitting a real failure, and making repair after you’ve turned on the child inside are evidence too, alongside the meals, the limits that protect, the appointments and the kept promises. Show your love by not retaliating, but don’t substitute not retaliating for loving the younger part.

Notice what each position teaches the others: a vow of love followed by blame when it’s doubted teaches that love depends on receiving it correctly. And keep in mind that the position that made the vow and the position that blames the child for not accepting the vow may be two separate positions, or they may be the same position, or they may be a blend. Don’t go by chronological age.

When a younger you becomes the defendant in your own head, would it be of any value to try and understand what you understood back then? Would it help to try and appreciate what options you could see and tolerate? Would any useful insight be gained by considering the consequences of your actions? Whilst acknowledging the harm you may have caused, and working to address and repair that harm, remember that punishing yourself now can’t go back and give the person you were then the capacity they were missing.

The two-hand practice

So here is a simple easy little bit of body work for connecting with your inner child. All you have to do is place one hand in the center of your chest. That hand is a physical connection to love. Now place your other hand just below that, at your solar plexis, that is where you can relate to your child.

Now begin sending love down to your child from your heart and just notice what comes up for you. It doesn't matter if something comes up or not, if there is resistance, meet it with love, and if you feel or see something, meet that with love too. Let it be a conversation with your child from your heart, not a performance.

Now remember when you do this, Love is on top and your child is on the bottom and you as the adult are right there with them.

The Nurturer

As a Nurturer, you bring warmth, and one of the most important things you can do is to enjoy your inner child. To sit back and not feel like you have to move their feelings, but actually say to them, “I’m really glad you are here in this moment.” Children need to be enjoyed, not just consoled when they are hurt.

“I know it’s okay for you to feel the way you are feeling.”

“I want you to know that I’m here for you.”

“Right now, you don’t have to do anything.”

“You are not too much.”

“It’s okay to be small. You can be small here with me.”

“It’s okay to be angry. You can be angry here.”

“It’s okay to be sad. You can be sad here.”

“I’m going to be here for you.”

The Protector

Your Protector is what turns that warmth into something the child can believe.

Then set boundaries together - it can be anything from, 'I will leave the unsafe conversation', 'I will stop texting the person who destabilizes us', 'I will eat today', 'I will get some sleep tonight', 'I will keep a small promise', or, 'I won't leave you alone with adult consequences'.

This is where inner-child work often turns into fluffy decoration - people talk lovingly to their inner child, but then send the destabilizing message, skip the meal, avoid the task, and break the promise. Trust begins when you actually handle the consequence.

If warmth isn't available, that's okay, a protective act can start the relationship. Make sure they are small enough to carry out, and look at what actually happened. If you don't do them, work out why - was it fear, exhaustion, lack of skills, a practical barrier, poor planning, etc.? Doing it without feeling better right away isn't automatically failure, and ticking it off a list doesn't prove it helped.

The Leader, Guide, or Guru

Working with the Leader function, who provides direction. You can give it the name you like: Leader, Guide, Guru, Wise One, Sage, Inner Teacher, Director, Higher Adult, etc. The name matters much less than whether it can point the whole system toward a life.

Invite it to give direction, even ask for something difficult, not in a way that expects you to be perfectly disciplined and not have any needs. Ask it to help you find a way to do the adult thing and ask for help, express a preference, allow a safe person to see your imperfections, etc. Find ways to get your need for closeness met without punishing the other person for needing space, and without erasing either of you. Etc.

Affirmations to support the Leader may include: “We are not only here to feel good.” “We are here to become whole.” “We are here to belong to life itself, not only to people who approve of us.” “We are here to serve truth, beauty, love, God, source, nature, universe, dharma, Tao, the benefit of all beings.” Etc.

Begin with the adult function you can actually reach; protection may come before warmth. Be sure that the direction serves your child’s growth, but doesn’t deprive your child of necessary care, play, support, etc.

Working with protectors

Feel free to use this parts language when you actually recognize a protective pattern, or when it’s useful to explore. A sensation, a distraction or an objection doesn’t tell you its own cause. Notice it first: hunger may just need food, skepticism may be reasonable, and a sentence may simply not fit.

Most people assume when approaching their inner child that the first thing they’ll encounter is…their inner child.

But more often than not, what you actually experience is numbness, cynicism, anger, hunger, the sudden urge to check your phone, a sexual urge, mental planning, sleepiness, dissociation, or the simple thought that “this is stupid”. I wouldn’t call those failures. They’re often the protector, the guard at the door, showing up in its usual charming way.

One important voice to become aware of when approaching your inner child is your inherited parent. This is the voice of your parent(s) that you internalized as a child, based on how they treated you. This is not the same as your inner adult (Nurturer, Protector, Leader/Guru) that you will eventually build up. Often this inherited parent acts as a critic or warden, telling your inner child not to cry, not to be “needy”, not to embarrass them, not to be too independent, etc. So when you begin talking to your child in a new, loving way, this voice may jump in to say that what you’re doing is “fake”.

“I notice you. You’re trying to protect something, and I want to understand. Can I ask you what you’re afraid would happen if you stopped?”

Now be patient, and listen. It may be that they’re afraid that you’ll lie to yourself again, or that this will turn into another performance, or that feeling the pain will destroy you, or that you’ll use spirituality to dodge reality, forgive too early, call a fantasy guidance, or leave them hanging the moment the session is over.

Now, tell the protective part that makes sense, that it doesn’t have to move yet, and ask what would help it trust you 1% more.

Usually the protector needs evidence more than another spiritual insight: things like maintaining a boundary, doing a certain task, eating properly, holding back from sending a text, keeping the promise, or sleeping, or reaching out to a therapist, or acknowledging that you do, in fact, owe someone money, or writing down the truth.

Protection that knows when to stop scanning

The Protector is more than an inner voice saying no. Want to “embody” it? Practice the following sequence:

(1) orient self (look around, feel support, etc.),

(2) assess situation (what do you know, not know, need to check out?),

(3) differentiate between actual/real dangers, uncertainty, past dangers or imagined dangers,

(4) set boundaries (just one, proportional to danger level; move, stop, delay, ask, leave, get support, etc.),

(5) verify enough safety (not perfect certainty, just enough real evidence for the next step), and finally

(6) stand down and rest: protecting includes ending the scan once more vigilance isn’t helping.

Seems to me that this would be a “mature” Protector. For example, it wouldn’t be afraid to say, “I don’t know”, or to ask another human being, or to delay interpreting what’s going on, or to use a no-trance practice. I want to be able to “do” this. I am learning discernment that acts when needed, and to quit scanning the room after the danger has passed.

Inner child reparenting

I connect my reparenting therapy to self hypnosis. I think they’re a perfect fit. So, while you are in hypnosis, the child may arrive (this can be any age, image, posture, voice, memory, emotion, vulnerable self, or no child at all. If there is no child, stay with a protector you recognize, or with whatever sensation, feeling or preference is actually there).

If there is a child that appears, don’t feel like you have to do anything with them. Just be with them.

See if you can tell the child: “Little one, I am here. You don’t have to explain everything, you don’t even have to be healed today. You don’t have to impress me. Just tell me if there’s something you need to help you feel less alone.”

It can be anything. Need warmth? need to play? need protection? need to grieve? need to be angry? need food? rest? a boundary? a safer relationship? need to stop fantasizing? need to stop working so hard? need me to keep a promise to you for one day?

Don’t rush the repair

Find a younger you /protector/feeling/signal in your body that needs tending to and then:

Prepare yourself to do the tending (Get yourself into a place where you have time, privacy, support etc. Be as adult as you can)

Look at what’s there before you decide what it means

Ask for permission to move closer or what is needed (warmth, space, words, silence, no contact etc)

Do something to meet one of the needs you find when you move closer. Don’t try to fix it all.

Wait a while for the effect of what you have done to sink in. Some changes need quiet, sleep or just ordinary time.

Reconnect with that part of you ( don’t expect it to become one with you, go away, forgive, or be happy, just connect if it wants to)

Rest, and stop before the care turns into another performance. Then come back later and ask what actually helped.

Your aim is not to make it all good as new, as if your history should disappear, but good as you: more supported and connected, and still recognizably yourself. Feel free to change the language if the part talk is not useful, think signal, feeling, younger you or anything that helps you connect with the issue

Play and rest still need an adult present

Reparenting doesn't have to be solemn. It's really okay to let your younger states enjoy playing with things that interest them. Touch textures, draw, move your body, talk to your plushie in a different voice, as long as you can keep reality testing intact and remember that you are not actually a child/pet/doll/whatever and are not owned, it's okay to recover your play ability.

Resting without being helpless: sometimes you just need to rest, and that doesn't have to mean being helpless. Cut down on decisions for a set period, put unfinished tasks somewhere you can see them, and let the adult in you keep watch. You can still move, stop and come back.

Non-dominant hand dialogue

If speaking or visualization feels fake, try writing. Have your non-dominant hand write as your child/protector (even if your handwriting looks a little awkward), and have your dominant hand answer as you. For example, your non-dominant hand might write, “I don’t trust you.” Answer with your dominant hand, “I hear that you don’t trust me, but I love you, and I want to know where I’ve let you down. I won’t ask you to trust me, but I want to hear you out and make one promise to you that I will keep today.” Your non-dominant hand might respond, “What promise?” Your dominant hand might write, “I will eat, clean the desk, and not text the person who makes us feel unsafe.”

Let the next response guide you

Having read the induction and participated in the inner meeting, you are ready to learn to respond rather than read a speech that has already decided what every part will say. Read the following examples before you practice without a screen.

Respond by giving an accurate noticing of one thing and a small, believable invitation (or an act of care, or more time). A sensation can lead to an image, a gesture, a feeling, or words. It doesn’t have to fill every one of those. Then acknowledge only what actually happens, and wait.

Finding your own words

Say you notice, "My chest tightened when I imagined asking for help." Start with that,

rather than deciding, "This must be an abandoned child / a protective mechanism." Then you might say: "And as I notice that tightening, I can give myself a little time before deciding what it means … and notice whether there’s something I’d like to say, change, or simply stay with."

Then listen. That’s enough language for one invitation. A plain "What happens next?" may be better than an elegant sentence. While a feeling is developing, it may be best to pause the words if that gives it room, and somedays the words help you understand, so keep them.

When that’s the help you chose, you can be quite firm with yourself: "Let the explanation wait a moment. What do I feel as I say that?" Being direct can focus your attention without deciding the answer. You can simply stay with a difficult feeling, rather than waiting until it has become pleasant. If you’re still present, can change direction, and want to continue, sadness or tension on its own doesn’t mean you have to stop. It can be ok to stay.

Keep apart "What I notice", "What it seems to mean to me", and "What I think about what it seems to mean." The boundaries between the three are fuzzy, and you don’t need to prove which came first. When it helps, ask: "What did I notice? What did it seem to mean? What supports or challenges that meaning?"

Is it a notice or a meaning? "It made my stomach tight" is a notice. "That person is evil" is a meaning. (even if it came as a wordless certainty). Ask what they actually did, what cues you noticed, and what else could explain the alarm. It's ok to use phrases you come up with later to analyze the meaning, not only phrases that appeared in your head at the time. Nonverbal or early thoughts are not necessarily more true or valuable. Feelings deserve attention, and what they mean is still open to analysis.

Let the response change the invitation

There is a difference between "my shoulders tightened" and "that wording feels wrong". Tightening on its own doesn't explain itself: ask what happened, and whether the invitation fits. A clear no doesn't need any more reasons; change the words, the pace, or the approach, and don't repeat the unwelcome suggestion more persuasively.

I notice the tightness. I can leave it as it is for a moment. Does this invitation fit, or would I prefer something different?

Sometimes the sentence was simply wrong. Sometimes it's something I hadn't considered, and the feeling is worth meeting. I don't have to decide which before I make space to find out. Skepticism isn't automatically a protector, and silence isn't proof that some hidden process is working.

Look at the situation too

When another person is involved, notice what they actually do before you make the whole problem an inner-child reaction. Can they hear disagreement, take responsibility, and make room for your experience? Be as specific as you can, and be ready to change your mind. Just “disagreeing” with you or setting boundaries doesn’t by itself show emotional immaturity. And you don’t need repeated exposure to a dangerous situation before you’re allowed to protect yourself.

Notice your side too. Guilt does not necessarily mean that you have done something wrong or were manipulated. Did you cause harm that needs repair, or did you drop your position to make their disappointment go away, or both? What’s a realistic aim for the next interaction? Sometimes it is mutual understanding but sometimes you need to just convey information, set boundaries, or cut the interaction short. You don’t have to make someone understand before you can act.

Change the amount of contact

When you need less, widen your attention to something easier: the room, the chair, a sound, or somewhere in your body that’s easier to meet. Let that support become noticeable alongside what is difficult for you. Going back and forth between what is difficult and what is easier is called pendulation. Doing a little bit at a time is called titration. You get to set the pace based on how you are doing. You don’t have to do a certain number.

Ok, I can let this much be here, and notice my support beside it.

Only come back to the difficult stuff when you choose to. If you find that you are losing track of the present, things are becoming more and more unreal for you, or you are unable to switch or stop what you are doing, then stop exploring within and use the full return. If you find that you are having trouble orienting for a prolonged period, then please get human help, not a stronger induction.

If you feel the urge to move, turn, reach, push, or change your body position, then feel free to either do something small that is not painful or uncomfortable to your body or imagine that you are doing it, and notice what follows. You do not need to act out the urge or feel that you must move, shake, or release. If you find that moving causes pain or symptoms that you are concerned about, then stop moving.

Offer the care that is actually wanted

When a younger feeling shows up, I offer it company without making it literally younger or asking it to explain its history. If I can recognize who the protector is, I listen to its concern, without demanding that it step aside. All are welcome in the meeting, and I don’t need them to go away, or even trust me right now.

I’m here for you if you want me to be. If you need some space, I can provide that also.

If they don’t want me to come closer, I just do what they ask, and see how that feels. If I notice that a Nurturer could be useful in changing the tone, or a Protector could help me set a boundary, or a Leader could help me see how to live my life better, they don’t each need a speech, I just borrow the function that I don’t have at that moment. (I only use the Witness if I need help getting started, otherwise I don’t re-do a step I already can do.)

I try different ways of supporting them – a welcome hand placement, an imagined presence, words they’d like to hear, changing my body position, moving further away etc., one change at a time, to see what it does. A resource that sounds comforting only earns its place if it actually helps right now.

Getting care now can bring up grief for what was missing back then. That doesn’t mean the love is failing. Allow yourself to respond as long as you want and as long as you can ‘stay there’. More tears don’t prove more healing. If the voice, closeness, touch, image, etc. seems intrusive then change it. Don’t think that you can’t ‘take’ the love.

Let a metaphor develop before you decide what it means. You could say, “If this problem had its own image or story, what would show up?” and, “what wants to happen next?” Try out ‘doing something’ that you feel would give you the resource that you feel you are missing, or set a boundary, move away, or take an action, only as far as it seems useful. Keep in mind that this information is symbolic and might be a good hypothesis for what you need but it’s not a proven fact about your history.

Or spend the session developing something you want: love, play, courage or curiosity. Let a pleasant experience have time to grow. Rehearse something you’ve decided to do, and notice what it would take to actually do it. Hypnosis can invite something new, not only listen to what’s already there.

Finish without forcing a revelation

Once you feel you've had enough, you can stop asking yourself new questions. However, it is a good idea to explore whether there's anything you can do to help you to leave things where they are for the time being. This might include thanking the parts or capacities you've been working with, in words you can actually mean. A meal, a boundary, rest, a repaired relationship or a promise kept may matter more than another insight. Or, it may be that there's nothing you need to do.

Throughout this exercise, your analytical mind is welcome to comment on what's going on, to not go along with something, or to stop the process. However, it's best to postpone any long checking of the facts, and any commitments that matter, until after you've returned. An image can be meaningful without being a historical memory, and just because you've seen an image or experienced a shift or release in your body doesn't mean that your interpretation of what's going on is correct.

Even if you ended the process early, use the Come all the way back procedure to return. Afterwards, write a few lines: what was there before, what you tried, what happened, and what's still uncertain. Include any memorable phrase that came up, any signals from your body, any needs expressed by a child part, any concerns expressed by a protector part, any boundaries you set, any repairs you made, or anything you learned that it would be a mistake to try to force, but only what actually appeared. You don't owe the notebook a complete cast of characters.

Appendix F: Self-trust, outside guidance, and oracle-like states

(See how to use synchronicity as a cue above.) It turns noticing into orientation and reality-testing, not an oracle.

People’s suggestibility varies hugely, both between individuals and according to state, whether you’re talking about external or internal suggestion, and the type of suggestion (commands, imagery, music, metaphors, spiritual etc). There are definitely advantages to both working with someone and doing it yourself, and it depends on what you’re trying to do. A professional can bring pacing, containment and another set of eyes, and doing it yourself gives you instant follow-up, real-time correction and a private line to your own protectors.

That said, self hypnosis may be the best way of talking to your subconscious on a day to day basis. If you’re dealing with particularly complicated trauma, blind spots, dissociation, destabilisation, or relational wounds that need another nervous system, skilled outside support may be best.

Finding a hypnotist who can work with you

Things to ask: What are they trained to treat? How do they use hypnosis in their practice? What will they do if something doesn’t “fit”? If you are working with trauma: Did they actually get training in trauma and dissociation in addition to whatever hypnosis certification they might have? (Remember, credentials matter, but they don’t guarantee competent care!)

Tell them what has and hasn’t worked for you in the past. How direct you want them to be. What kind of touch (if any) you are ok with. What kind of imagery (if any) you are ok with. What to do if you want to stop a session. And ask them what they do about unexpected reactions in or after a session, about things you aren’t sure are memories, and how they do the full return at the end. Keep in mind that a good person should be able to firmly encourage you without making it continue if you say you don’t want to.

Afterwards, look at what actually happened, not the method’s name. Why they used it (if they said). Whether or not you agreed to it. How the person responded to you (again, keep in mind that discomfort doesn’t mean it was “bad,” but seeing your objections as meaning you needed more of the same might be worth looking into). You can ask the app or others knowledgeable about dissociation and trauma to help explain what happened, but it is unlikely someone can tell you if the person was “certified” or not just based on what you tell them. Depending on what you find out, you might want to try self-hypnosis, combining the two, or finding another practitioner. Those stay your choices.

When the subconscious speaks like an oracle

The subconscious can notice things the conscious mind misses. Anticipations, pattern reads, or just things that seem a bit uncanny that come from it should be respected. The subconscious may send out the image of something or tell you to do something, but that does n't mean it is an order.

If it is something big, or can not be undone easily, it needs to be slowed down to the scale of its consequences, looked at with the adult’s questions, and brought to a council.

The council — internal first, then outward

First go within; ask the child in you, the adult in you, the conscious and subconscious minds, your intuition and analysis. But if the thing is larger than any of those, go outside for more help. The bigger and more irreversible the move, the more you need to look outside.

Go to people who love you, people who are like you, or people who have traveled that path. Of course sometimes going alone is the right thing, but I would do that as a last step, after first seeking counsel.

On the other hand, it is possible to give your power away. Seeking counsel can quietly turn into abdicating to an authority figure. Another person doesn’t get automatic trust, or automatic dismissal.

Sometimes you need the support of your peers. In Hearthwork, the concept is that you give each other equal time, warmth, confidentiality, and acceptance of “no” as an answer, and you act for each other as Nurturer and Protector, but not as Guide. Then you reverse roles. Sometimes, with a question asked carefully and at the right time, your peers can help you hear your own Guide more clearly, but they don’t interpret what you experience.

Forgiveness without bypass

We can’t “force” forgiveness, it has to come from a place of understanding, otherwise it becomes a bypass. And yet staying angry forever can let the injury keep running the present. How do we hold all of this? It can all be true together: the harm happened, the boundary still matters, the person is still accountable, and forgiveness may come later, when your relationship to what happened changes on its own.

A helpful understanding to come to, is that while their actions were harmful, in a sense, they could only make the moves they made, given their accumulated nature at the time (conditioning, history, pain, capacity, etc). This doesn’t negate that harm was caused, holding someone accountable, allowing for consequences, working on making different moves now, etc. It simply helps us come to a place where we aren’t expecting something from someone that they can’t give. It doesn’t make their limitations matter any less.

“You don’t have to forgive before you’re ready. I won’t use spirituality to silence your pain. And I won’t build our whole life around this wound forever.”

Some questions that may be helpful to ask when coming to a place of forgiveness, while still holding all of the above:

What actually happened? What was the impact? What boundaries need to be set? What shaped the other person(s) into someone capable of that harm? What is theirs? What is mine? What does accountability require? How can I let this go, without denying any of the above?

For self-forgiveness, name what you did, without taking responsibility for what wasn't yours. Let the remorse register the harm, or how it went against your values, without making yourself a permanent criminal.

Take responsibility, feel the remorse, then rectify if you can, and then let it go. Be specific about the action you took, and the impact it had, feel the remorse, do what you can to rectify or keep it from happening again, and then stop holding yourself hostage.

Introduction

Hello Lovey Bunny!

Have you ever considered the fact that you were born with a brain and mind that is capable of many different layers of consciousness: dreaming, protecting, analyzing, imitating, loving, remembering, hiding, revealing and healing, etc. etc.?

Instead of learning how to integrate all of these different layers, you were taught (and/or you learned on your own) how to push through, repress or supress your emotions, to pretend to be confident, to follow or defy authority, and so on and so forth, and to call that adulthood. Meanwhile, your deeper mind kept running its own "programs": the child mind wanting safety, the guard expecting danger, the body mind remembering what you explained away, the intuitive mind speaking before words, the fantasy mind trying to become guidance, etc.

A lot of hypnosis teaching acts as if the subconscious mind worked like a machine, and all you had to do was feed in a command and the machine would do what you put in. That never did much for me. For me, a much more useful model was to sit down and listen to the different parts of myself (the scared kid, the guard, the body, the intuition, the part trying to run Tuesday) until they all could be heard without one of them seizing the microphone.

This guide teaches a method of self-hypnosis that gathers your attention and brings the conscious mind, subconscious mind, body, inner child, protector parts, the adult self, and the Higher Self all into the same room to be able to listen and talk together honestly.

Where do I start? Easy. Just listen, warm up to, protect, clarify, reality test and act on it!

It doesn’t have to be a dramatic trance experience but it does have to lead to a more trustworthy relationship between all parts of the mind, proven in ordinary life.

Let’s call it communion. The conscious mind doesn’t have to shout it’s message from the roof top and the subconscious doesn’t have to rely on symptoms, dreams, cravings, day dreams, and other weird body signals to communicate.

I work with the premise that the subconscious is a living ecology of parts, memories, impulses, images, protections and wisdom. When the system needs coherence, I begin with Higher Self or the universal heart, and I separate into those parts only when that helps. I bring in inner-child reparenting because a wounded young part won’t be repaired by a clever suggestion. I also pull in elements from prompt engineering, because the shape of a question changes the kind of answer we can hear, and teach literacy in the domain of influence, since hypnosis is far from the only thing that’s hypnotizing us.

Closing

I believe that your subconscious mind, your body, your sharp analytical mind, and the protector that has been braced for years aren’t your enemies. Most of them have been trying to help without ever being properly introduced.

How deeply you can “get hypnotized” isn’t as important to me as whether or not you can become an adult you can trust.

Then listen until the kid is willing to come closer. It’s easiest if you keep enough small promises to the kid, because then the guards can relax a bit. Work on loving yourself, so that your thought processes don’t fight it, and work on thinking clearly, so that your love doesn’t slip off into fantasy. Work on applying this to your regular life, too, so that your adult can keep the promise.

Appendix D: Anxiety — body first

Remember that the anxiety is often coming from a part of yourself that is a Protector who believes they are trying to protect yourself from danger, shame, abandonment, failure, exposure, illness, rejection, losing control, or something that the protector believes will be unbearable for yourself. Rather than getting into a dialogue where it feels as though yourself is interrogating the protector, start with yourself by taking care of the body.

Always work with yourself by taking care of the body first, then the inner child, then doing some inner inquiry work, and then taking some kind of action.

Inner child love

Start by putting your hand over your heart and your other hand on your solar plexis and say lovingly, “Little one, you are not alone. You don’t have to fix this. I’m here now. The adult is listening.”

Don’t say the words, just hoping that they will work on your subconscious mind. Say them to yourself like you are talking to a frightened little child that you love.

Reduced breathing / Buteyko-style breathing

NOTE: There are some good things to be said for slowing down the breathing, for some people who overbreathe or are subject to panic. Some of this is based on the Buteyko approach. However, don’t force breath holds, and creating air hunger can increase anxiety for a short period. Take things slowly.

Try breathing through the nose. Try small inhales. Try quiet exhales. Try pausing if it is comfortable. See if it is possible to quiet the breathing. STOP if this creates dizziness, strain, a sense of panic or any other medical concerns.

EFT tapping

One of the simplest aspects of EFT is that it’s something you can do in your body. If you’re worried about something, you can name it, tap gently on your body, and get in touch with the feeling. There isn’t a ton of evidence, but a 2025 systematic review of EFT and anxiety disorders found seven randomized control trials and noted that EFT was more effective than no intervention in several studies. Still, the evidence should be handled with a bit of caution next to first-line therapies.

Gendlin Focusing

“What is the felt sense of this whole anxiety?”

Don’t answer from your head right away. Give your body time to get one vague sense of the whole thing. Then, ask:

“What would this felt sense like me to know?”

Try out a word or phrase to see if it fits, but also look at what it says about the situation. A word that feels ok might say something that doesn’t fit. It’s good to use both, the words and the body, to correct each other.

Body supports

Sometimes the mind is too activated to let meditation to take care of it. It may be useful to start from the body instead. Consider massage. Maybe massage a foot, or the scalp, or a temple, or the back of the neck, or the top of a shoulder. (Avoid the front of the neck. Avoid injured, numb, bruised, inflamed, recently surgically-operated-on areas, and varicose veins. Stop if it makes the anxiety symptoms or anything else feel bad, such as painful, dizzy, tingly, etc.) Other body approaches that may help include heat, pressure, weighted blanket, darkness, favorite calming music, massage gun used carefully, etc.

Others settle with warmth, darkness, favorite music, massage, weighted blanket, breathwork, favorite object, or personal relaxation technology. Use the support that actually helps, rather than building a tiny wellness trade show around the anxiety.

See my ZHoly3O page for more on the use of ozonated charcoal, “holy water” as one relaxation support. I also mention Blushield there, and both are optional, not at all essential. Neither one proves that any inner signal is true. The important thing is to get the body to a state of stabilization, listen gently, reality-test the messages from the “inner realm”, and come back to one grounded action.

Anxiety script

First, where is my body? What are my feet doing? How am I sitting in the chair? How am I breathing? What is my body doing in this room?

And if you can hear me, little one, know that I am here. Thank you, protector, for alerting me. You do not need to scream. I got the message.

Now if there is real action needed, show me the first step to take right now. And if no action is needed, help my body stand down gently.

I won’t abandon the signal, but I won’t worship it either. I’ll listen, test, and act.
